claim: Most mutations in MLC1 result in the degradation of the encoded protein MLC1
source: Most mutations in MLC1 result in the degradation of the encoded protein MLC1 (Duarri et al., 2008; Lanciotti et al., 2016; Leegwater et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations (Duarri et al., 2008; Lanciotti et al., 2016; Leegwater et al., 2001).

claim: MLC patients present widespread brain edema and swollen perivascular astrocytic processes
source: Indeed, MLC patients present widespread brain edema and swollen perivascular astrocytic processes (Bugiani et al., 2017; Dubey et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Bugiani et al., 2017; Dubey et al., 2015).

claim: MLC1 expression in mouse perivascular astrocytic processes starts around postnatal day 5
source: We recently reported that MLC1 expression in mouse perivascular astrocytic processes starts around postnatal day (P) 5 and that the MLC1/GlialCAM complex forms progressively from P5 to P15, with the protein deposits creating a meshwork between the astrocytes' perivascular membranes (Gilbert et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Gilbert et al., 2019).

claim: The MLC1/GlialCAM complex forms progressively from P5 to P15 in mice
source: We recently reported that MLC1 expression in mouse perivascular astrocytic processes starts around postnatal day (P) 5 and that the MLC1/GlialCAM complex forms progressively from P5 to P15, with the protein deposits creating a meshwork between the astrocytes' perivascular membranes (Gilbert et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Gilbert et al., 2019).

claim: The postnatal period P5-P15 is a developmental window for the molecular maturation of brain endothelial cells
source: We also demonstrated that this postnatal period is a developmental window for the molecular maturation of brain endothelial cells, particularly with regard to their efflux properties and for the contractility of vascular smooth muscle cells (Gilbert et al., 2019; Slaoui et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Gilbert et al., 2019; Slaoui et al., 2021).

claim: Astrocytes are key regulators of cerebrovascular development and function
source: Given that astrocytes are key regulators of cerebrovascular development and function (e.g., blood–brain barrier integrity, immune quiescence and perivascular homeostasis, neurovascular coupling) (Abbott et al., 2006; Alvarez et al., 2013; Castro Dias et al., 2019; Cohen-Salmon et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by four citations (Abbott et al., 2006; Alvarez et al., 2013; Castro Dias et al., 2019; Cohen-Salmon et al., 2021).

claim: The apparent diffusion coefficient was higher in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice
source: We first observed that the apparent diffusion coefficient (measured using magnetic resonance imaging) was higher in Mlc1 KO mice (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and related supplementary figures.

claim: The volume of the ventricles and the brain was larger in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice
source: Furthermore, the volume of the ventricles and the brain estimated from the anatomical T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging acquisition was larger in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The vascular volume measured by in situ brain perfusion of [14C] sucrose was the same in Mlc1 KO and WT mice
source: Indeed, the vascular volume measured by in situ brain perfusion of [14C] sucrose (a marker of vascular space and integrity; Dagenais et al., 2000) was the same in Mlc1 KO and WT mice and so suggested that the blood–brain barrier was not leaky, even in the shear stress conditions (increased hydrostatic pressure: 180 mmHg) produced by the addition of human serum albumin to the perfusate (Ezan et al., 2012; Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citations (Dagenais et al., 2000; Ezan et al., 2012).

claim: There were no differences between WT and Mlc1 KO mice in vessel length, branching, and tortuosity in the parenchymal or pial vasculature
source: There were no differences between WT and Mlc1 KO mice with regard to these architectural parameters in either the parenchymal or pial vasculature at the cortical surface (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The absence of MLC1 leads to fluid accumulation in the brain
source: Hence, the absence of MLC1 leads to fluid accumulation in the brain but has no obvious impact on the postnatal molecular maturation of ECs, blood–brain barrier integrity, or endothelium architecture.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The absence of MLC1 has no obvious impact on the postnatal molecular maturation of endothelial cells
source: Hence, the absence of MLC1 leads to fluid accumulation in the brain but has no obvious impact on the postnatal molecular maturation of ECs, blood–brain barrier integrity, or endothelium architecture.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Acta2 mRNA was significantly downregulated in Mlc1 KO mice on P5 and P15
source: In Mlc1 KO mice, however, Acta2 was significantly downregulated on P5 and P15, while Atp1b1 levels were unchanged (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A small decrease in SMA expression was found in Mlc1 KO microvessels from P15 onward, becoming significant only at P60
source: A small decrease in SMA expression was found in Mlc1 KO microvessels from P15 onward, although it became significant only at P60.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Additional bands of lower molecular weights resembling a degradation pattern were detected in Mlc1 KO mice at P60
source: Moreover, additional bands of lower molecular weights resembling a degradation pattern were detected at this stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No discontinuities in SMA labeling were detected in the parenchymal or pial vasculature in Mlc1 KO mice
source: No discontinuities in the labeling were detected in the parenchymal (Figure 2C) or pial vasculature (at the cortical surface) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The SMA-positive vessels' length, branching, tortuosity, and number of anastomoses were the same in Mlc1 KO and WT mice
source: Moreover, the SMA-positive vessels' length, branching, tortuosity, and number of anastomoses (analyzed only in pial vessels) were the same in Mlc1 KO and WT mice (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The absence of MLC1 perturbs the developmental expression of SMA but does not affect the development of the vascular smooth muscle cell network
source: These findings indicate that the absence of MLC1 perturbs the developmental expression of SMA but does not affect the development of the vascular smooth muscle cell network.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The amplitude and speed of vasoconstriction were significantly lower in Mlc1 KO mice from P15 onward
source: Strikingly, the amplitude and speed of vasoconstriction were significantly lower in Mlc1 KO mice from P15 onward (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ex vivo vasomotor response data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The postnatal acquisition of contractility is impaired in the absence of MLC1
source: These results indicate that the postnatal acquisition of contractility is impaired in the absence of MLC1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Mlc1 KO mice displayed significantly lower blood perfusion, suggesting narrower penetrating arteries
source: Mlc1 KO mice displayed significantly lower blood perfusion, suggesting narrower penetrating arteries (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ultrasound localization microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The increase in cerebral blood flow evoked by whisker stimulation was significantly smaller in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice
source: The increase in cerebral blood flow evoked by whisker stimulation was significantly smaller in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice, indicating that neurovascular coupling was impaired in the KO mice (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional ultrasound imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Neurovascular coupling was impaired in Mlc1 KO mice
source: The increase in cerebral blood flow evoked by whisker stimulation was significantly smaller in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice, indicating that neurovascular coupling was impaired in the KO mice (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional ultrasound imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The absence of MLC1 impairs the postnatal acquisition of contractile properties by vascular smooth muscle cells
source: In conclusion, the absence of MLC1 impairs the postnatal acquisition of contractile properties by vascular smooth muscle cells and impedes blood perfusion, vessel diameter, and neurovascular coupling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: GlialCAM was not detected around vessels in Mlc1 KO mice at any stage
source: GlialCAM (whose location at the astrocyte endfoot membrane and immunolabeling depends on MLC1) was not detected around vessel in Mlc1 KO mice at any stage, as described previously (Hoegg-Beiler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and a citation (Hoegg-Beiler et al., 2014).

claim: Perivascular Aqp4 and Cx43 were almost undetectable on P5 in Mlc1 KO mice but were detected on perivascular astrocytic membranes from P15 onward
source: Interestingly, perivascular Aqp4 and Cx43 were almost undetectable on P5 in Mlc1 KO mice but were detected on perivascular astrocytic membranes from P15 onward (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Kir4.1 was present on perivascular astrocytic membranes in Mlc1 KO mice, although the immunofluorescence was less intense
source: Kir4.1 was present on perivascular astrocytic membranes in Mlc1 KO mice, although the immunofluorescence was less intense.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In Mlc1 KO mice, lower levels of Aqp4, Cx43, and GlialCAM were observed on P5 only
source: In Mlc1 KO mice, we observed lower levels of Aqp4, Cx43, and GlialCAM on P5 only and lower levels of Kir4.1 on P15 and P60 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Lower levels of Kir4.1 were observed in Mlc1 KO mice on P15 and P60
source: In Mlc1 KO mice, we observed lower levels of Aqp4, Cx43, and GlialCAM on P5 only and lower levels of Kir4.1 on P15 and P60 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Mlc1 KO mice, the perivascular Cx43 puncta were larger and denser
source: In the Mlc1 KO mice, however, the perivascular Cx43 puncta were larger and denser (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Kir4.1 perivascular puncta were the same size in both WT and Mlc1 KO samples but were less dense in Mlc1 KO mice
source: Kir4.1 perivascular puncta were the same size in both the WT and Mlc1 KO samples but were less dense in Mlc1 KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The absence of MLC1 is associated with lower expression of Kir4.1
source: These results show that the absence of MLC1 is associated with lower expression of Kir4.1, the delayed expression of Aqp4 and Cx43, the disruption (from P5 onward) of the GlialCAM's membrane anchoring, and impairment of Cx43's perivascular organization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The absence of MLC1 is associated with delayed expression of Aqp4 and Cx43
source: These results show that the absence of MLC1 is associated with lower expression of Kir4.1, the delayed expression of Aqp4 and Cx43, the disruption (from P5 onward) of the GlialCAM's membrane anchoring, and impairment of Cx43's perivascular organization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: MLC1 is required for the development and maintenance of the perivascular astrocytic processes' molecular organization
source: The data suggest that MLC1 is required for the development and maintenance of the perivascular astrocytic processes' molecular organization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The level of Aqp4 in the extract of mechanically purified brain microvessels was significantly lower in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice
source: However, the level of Aqp4 in the extract of mechanically purified brain microvessels was significantly lower in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NF-M was similarly present in whole-brain extracts from WT and Mlc1 KO mice but was significantly less present in P60 Mlc1 KO microvessels
source: The same was true for neurofilament protein M (NF-M), a neuronal-specific intermediate filament protein present in neuronal fibers abutting perivascular astrocytic processes. NF-M was similarly present in whole-brain extracts from WT and Mlc1 KO mice but was significantly less present in P60 Mlc1 KO microvessels (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The perivascular astrocytic processes and the associated neuronal fibers had detached from Mlc1 KO brain vessels when the latter were mechanically purified
source: These data suggested that the perivascular astrocytic processes and the associated neuronal fibers had detached from Mlc1 KO brain vessels when the latter were mechanically purified.
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data showing lower levels of Aqp4 and NF-M in purified microvessels.

claim: In the Mlc1 KO sample, Aqp4 and NF-M immunolabeling present at the surface of the purified vessels was discontinuous and less intense than in the WT sample
source: In the Mlc1 KO sample, Aqp4 and NF-M immunolabeling present at the surface of the purified vessels was discontinuous and less intense than in the WT sample (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: MLC1 influences the mechanical cohesiveness of perivascular astrocytic processes at the vessel surface
source: Taken as a whole, these results suggest that MLC1 influences the mechanical cohesiveness of perivascular astrocytic processes at the vessel surface (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Mlc1 KO astrocytes displayed a greater number of processes located between 15 and 25 µm from the soma
source: Mlc1 KO astrocytes displayed a greater number of processes located between 15 and 25 µm from the soma (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both Mlc1 KO and WT astrocytes were equally well oriented with respect to the pyramidal cell layer, with a polarity index >1
source: We found that both Mlc1 KO and WT astrocytes were equally well oriented, with a polarity index >1 (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by polarity analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When taking hippocampal vessels as the reference, Mlc1 KO astrocytes were abnormally oriented toward vessels in the axial plane
source: However, when taking hippocampal vessels as the reference, Mlc1 KO astrocytes were abnormally oriented toward vessels in the axial plane (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by polarity analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MLC1 is required for the development and maintenance of astrocyte morphology and polarity
source: Taken as a whole, these results indicate that MLC1 is required for the development and maintenance of astrocyte morphology and polarity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: In WT mice, endothelial cells were joined by tight junctions and were totally covered by perivascular astrocytic processes
source: In WT mice, endothelial cells were joined by tight junctions and were totally covered by perivascular astrocytic processes, which themselves were joined by gap junctions.
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In Mlc1 KO mice, the endothelium appeared to be unaltered: normal tight junctions and basal lamina, and no accumulation of intracellular vesicles
source: In Mlc1 KO mice, the endothelium appeared to be unaltered: normal tight junctions and basal lamina, and no accumulation of intracellular vesicles (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: The astrocytes' perivascular organization was drastically modified in Mlc1 KO mice
source: However, the astrocytes' perivascular organization was drastically modified (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: Perivascular astrocytic processes surrounded by basal lamina were observed in Mlc1 KO mice
source: We observed perivascular astrocytic processes surrounded by basal lamina (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perivascular astrocytic processes stacked on top of each other and joined by gigantic gap junction plaques were observed in Mlc1 KO mice
source: or stacked on top of each other and joined by gigantic gap junction plaques (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No swelling was observed in Mlc1 KO perivascular astrocytic processes at P60
source: No swelling was observed in Mlc1 KO perivascular astrocytic processes (Figure 7B–E and G, Figure 7—source data 1) (edematous perivascular astrocytic processes were observed in 1-year-old Mlc1 KO mice; Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B-E and G.

claim: Edematous perivascular astrocytic processes were observed in 1-year-old Mlc1 KO mice
source: No swelling was observed in Mlc1 KO perivascular astrocytic processes (Figure 7B–E and G, Figure 7—source data 1) (edematous perivascular astrocytic processes were observed in 1-year-old Mlc1 KO mice; Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Astrocyte coverage in Mlc1 KO mice was often discontinuous
source: Strikingly, astrocyte coverage in Mlc1 KO mice was often discontinuous.
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: In the free spaces in Mlc1 KO mice, axons and synapses were found to be in direct contact with the endothelial basal lamina
source: In the free spaces, axons (recognizable by their microtubules) (Figure 7B and E) and synapses (recognizable by the large number of vesicles in the presynaptic part and their electron dense postsynaptic density (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)) were found to be in direct contact with the endothelial basal lamina.
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B, E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage of microvessels in which the endothelial basal lamina was in direct contact with at least one neuronal process was higher in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice
source: Accordingly, the percentage of microvessels in which the endothelial basal lamina was in direct contact with at least one neuronal process was higher in Mlc1 KO mice than in WT mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: On P5, the perivascular astrocytic processes covered about half of the vessel's circumference
source: On P5, the perivascular astrocytic processes covered about half of the vessel's circumference, and the WT and Mlc1 KO samples did not differ significantly in this respect (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The perivascular astrocyte coverage increased dramatically between P5 and P15 and was almost complete on P15 in WT mice
source: The perivascular astrocyte coverage increased dramatically between P5 and P15 and was almost complete on P15 in WT mice (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Mlc1 KO mice displayed a lower percentage of perivascular astrocytic process coverage from P10 onward
source: In contrast, Mlc1 KO mice displayed a lower percentage of perivascular astrocytic process coverage from P10 onward, and a large number of neuronal processes were inserted into the noncovered areas of the vessels (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The perivascular astrocyte coverage increases rapidly between P5 and P15
source: Our results demonstrate for the first time that the perivascular astrocyte coverage increases rapidly between P5 and P15.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: The perivascular astrocyte coverage process is impaired in Mlc1 KO mice
source: This process is impaired in Mlc1 KO mice and results in incomplete perivascular astrocytic process coverage and direct contact between infiltrating neuronal processes and the endothelial basal lamina (the processes normally remain behind the perivascular astrocyte layer).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: MLC1 is critical for the normal postnatal development of perivascular astrocyte coverage
source: Taken as a whole, these results indicate that (i) the absence of MLC1 in the gliovascular unit greatly alters the perivascular astrocytic processes' morphology and coverage and (ii) MLC1 is critical for the normal postnatal development of perivascular astrocyte coverage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Relative to WT mice, the mean DOTA-Gd concentration in Mlc1 KO mice was lower in the midbrain
source: Relative to WT mice, the mean DOTA-Gd concentration in Mlc1 KO mice was lower in the midbrain (Figure 8E, Figure 8—source data 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by magnetic resonance imaging data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The slope of DOTA-Gd dispersion was lower in Mlc1 KO mice in the cerebellum, midbrain, and cortex
source: and the slope was lower in the cerebellum, midbrain, and cortex (Figure 8D, E and G, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by magnetic resonance imaging data shown in Figure 8D, E, and G.

claim: The absence of MLC1 impairs the intraparenchymal circulation and clearance of CSF
source: We therefore conclude that the absence of MLC1 impairs the intraparenchymal circulation and clearance of CSF.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: Perivascular MLC1 was detected as early as 15 weeks of gestation in human cortical sections
source: Interestingly, perivascular MLC1 was detected as early as 15 weeks of gestation (Figure 9A, Figure 9—source data 1) and remained stable thereafter (Figure 9B–F, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In humans, the MLC1/GlialCAM complex and the astrocyte's perivascular coverage are initiated prenatally
source: These results suggested that in humans the MLC1/GlialCAM complex and the astrocyte's perivascular coverage are initiated prenatally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemical data showing early perivascular MLC1 expression in human fetal brain.

claim: The P5–P15 time window is important for the formation of perivascular astrocyte coverage in mice
source: Our previous research showed that, in the mouse, the MLC1/GlialCAM complex forms progressively after birth (between P5 and P15) (Gilbert et al., 2019). Our present work demonstrated for the first time that the P5–P15 time window is also important for the formation of perivascular astrocyte coverage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and previous work (Gilbert et al., 2019).

claim: On P5, perivascular astrocytic processes covered only 50% of the vascular surface
source: On P5, perivascular astrocytic processes covered only 50% of the vascular surface, and this coverage increased rapidly until completion on P15.
evidence: This is based on the quantitative analysis of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Perivascular astrocyte coverage increased rapidly until completion on P15 in WT mice
source: On P5, perivascular astrocytic processes covered only 50% of the vascular surface, and this coverage increased rapidly until completion on P15.
evidence: This is based on the quantitative analysis of transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The absence of MLC1 impairs the developmental process of perivascular astrocyte coverage
source: We show that the absence of MLC1 impairs this developmental process together with the astrocytic perivascular processes' molecular maturation, with a lower Kir4.1 expression and a transient decrease in Aqp4 and Cx43 protein levels on P5.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: From P10 onward, perivascular astrocytic processes incompletely cover the vessels in Mlc1 KO mice
source: From P10 onward, perivascular astrocytic processes incompletely cover the vessels and direct contact between neuronal components and the vessel wall are observed.
evidence: This is based on the transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Direct contact between neuronal components and the vessel wall are observed in Mlc1 KO mice from P10 onward
source: From P10 onward, perivascular astrocytic processes incompletely cover the vessels and direct contact between neuronal components and the vessel wall are observed.
evidence: This is based on the transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7B, E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The postnatal period is an intense synaptogenic phase in the mouse brain
source: Interestingly, the postnatal period is also an intense synaptogenic phase in the mouse brain (Chung et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Chung et al., 2015).

claim: Astrocytes and neurons might compete for the perivascular space during the postnatal period
source: astrocytes and neurons might compete for the perivascular space during this time.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that the postnatal period is a time of both astrocyte coverage development and synaptogenesis.

claim: In the absence of MLC1, neurons might either stabilize or insert into the space left free by perivascular astrocytic processes
source: In the absence of MLC1, neurons might either stabilize or insert into the space left free by perivascular astrocytic processes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of neuronal processes in direct contact with the endothelial basal lamina in Mlc1 KO mice.

claim: Disorganization of Cx43 was recently reported in GlialCAM KO mice
source: Interestingly, disorganization of Cx43 was recently reported in GlialCAM KO mice (Baldwin et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Baldwin et al., 2021).

claim: The MLC1/GlialCAM complex organizes gap junction coupling in perivascular astrocytic processes
source: this supports the hypothesis whereby the MLC1/GlialCAM complex organizes gap junction coupling in perivascular astrocytic processes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of Cx43 disorganization in both Mlc1 KO and GlialCAM KO mice.

claim: The astrocyte arborization becomes more complex between P7 and P21
source: It was recently demonstrated that the astrocyte arborization becomes more complex between P7 and P21 – the period during which the perivascular MLC1/GlialCAM astrocytic complex forms (Clavreul et al., 2019; Gilbert et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by two citations (Clavreul et al., 2019; Gilbert et al., 2019).

claim: The formation of perivascular astrocytic process coverage mediated by the MLC1/GliaCAM complex might influence astrocyte arborization and thus polarize astrocytes
source: The formation of perivascular astrocytic process coverage (mediated by the MLC1/GliaCAM complex) might influence this process and thus polarize astrocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the temporal correlation between MLC1/GlialCAM complex formation and astrocyte arborization.

claim: The incomplete perivascular astrocyte coverage, the abnormal astrocytic polarity, and the loss of the perivascular astrocytic processes' mechanical cohesiveness did not alter blood–brain barrier's integrity in Mlc1 KO
source: Although astrocytes are key regulators of the blood–brain barrier's integrity (Abbott et al., 2006; Alvarez et al., 2013; Castro Dias et al., 2019; Cohen-Salmon et al., 2021), the incomplete perivascular astrocyte coverage, the abnormal astrocytic polarity, and the loss of the perivascular astrocytic processes' mechanical cohesiveness did not alter blood–brain barrier's integrity in Mlc1 KO.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly the in situ brain perfusion data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The changes in perivascular astrocytic processes in Mlc1 KO mice probably alter the 'barrier' formed by perivascular astrocytic processes around the vessels
source: Nevertheless, these changes probably alter the 'barrier' formed by perivascular astrocytic processes around the vessels.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed changes in perivascular astrocytic processes.

claim: The changes in perivascular astrocytic processes in Mlc1 KO mice might greatly affect perivascular homeostasis and astrocyte signaling toward the vascular compartment
source: In turn, this might greatly affect perivascular homeostasis and astrocyte signaling toward the vascular compartment (Abbott et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed changes in perivascular astrocytic processes and supported by citations (Abbott et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2020).

claim: The astrocytes' perivascular organization is thought to be crucial for regulating the fluxes of CSF and interstitial fluid into the parenchyma
source: The astrocytes' perivascular organization is thought to be crucial for regulating the fluxes of CSF and interstitial fluid into the parenchyma (Abbott et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Abbott et al., 2018).

claim: Perivascular astrocytic process alterations in Mlc1 KO mice might be directly linked to the loss of DOTA-Gd intraparenchymal drainage observed
source: Perivascular astrocytic process alterations in Mlc1 KO mice might therefore be directly linked to the loss of DOTA-Gd intraparenchymal drainage observed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed changes in perivascular astrocytic processes and the DOTA-Gd drainage data.

claim: Megalencephaly in Mlc1 KO mice may alter the brain's drainage capacity by reducing the volume of subarachnoid spaces
source: By reducing the volume of subarachnoid spaces, megalencephaly in Mlc1 KO mice may also alter the brain's drainage capacity, as suggested by the lower level of DOTA-Gd transport into the CSF observed in Mlc1 KO mice.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed megalencephaly and the DOTA-Gd drainage data.

claim: Impaired parenchymal circulation of the CSF/interstitial fluid might contribute to the fluid accumulation and megalencephaly in Mlc1 KO mice
source: In the presence of an intact blood–brain barrier, impaired parenchymal circulation of the CSF/interstitial fluid might (i) contribute to the fluid accumulation and megalencephaly (Dubey et al., 2015; van der Knaap et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed impaired CSF/interstitial fluid circulation and supported by citations (Dubey et al., 2015; van der Knaap et al., 2012).

claim: Impaired parenchymal circulation of the CSF/interstitial fluid might lead to the progressive accumulation of harmful molecules in the brain
source: (ii) lead to the progressive accumulation of harmful molecules in the brain
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed impaired CSF/interstitial fluid circulation.

claim: Impaired parenchymal circulation of the CSF/interstitial fluid might increase susceptibility to neural disorders
source: and (iii) thus increase susceptibility to neural disorders (Rasmussen et al., 2018).
